glosses: A sudden or unsteady movement.

examples.text: the lurch of a ship, or of a drunkard

The ship was driving rapidly towards the rocky coast, against which she must have been dashed to pieces had she kept afloat a few minutes longer, but she gave a lurch and went down, rose again for an instant, and with another lurch sank, and all was over,—and there were nearly two hundred and fifty human beings struggling with the waves.

Yet I hoped by grouting at the earth below it to be able to dislodge the stone at the side; but while I was considering how best to begin, the candle flickered, the wick gave a sudden lurch to one side, and I was left in darkness.

glosses: To make such a sudden, unsteady movement.

examples.text: It occurred to me there was no time to lose, and dodging the boom as it once more lurched across the deck, I slipped aft and down the companion stairs into the cabin.
The incident made it think, apparently, that the neighborhood was dangerous, for it slowly lurched off through the wood, followed by its mate and its three enormous infants.
Number One lurched forward, his arms outstretched toward the horror stricken girl.
He was looking for trouble. He lurched against a table at which three soldiers were sitting and knocked over a glass of beer.

glosses: To swallow or eat greedily; to devour; hence, to swallow up.

examples.text: Too far off from great cities, which may hinder business; too near them, which lurcheth all provisions, and maketh everything dear.

glosses: To evade by stooping; to lurk; lie in wait; go about in a sneaking way.
To take by surprise; to unexpectedly detain.
To rob.

examples.text: And in the brunt of seventeen battles since / He lurched all swords of the garland.

glosses: A lift or heave.
A predicament or difficult situation.

examples.text: to leave someone in the lurch

glosses: An old game played with dice and counters; a variety of the game of tables.
A double score in cribbage for the winner when their adversary has not yet pegged their 31st hole.

examples.text:
August 14, 1784, Horace Walpole, letter to the Hon. H. S. Conway
Lady Blandford has cried her eyes out on losing a lurch.

glosses: To defeat in the game of cribbage with a lurch (double score as explained under noun entry).
To leave someone in the lurch; to cheat.

examples.text: Never deceive or lurch the sincere communicant.

translations.source_sense_description: meist über ein Fahrzeug: sich ruckartig, unruhig bewegen, weil der Untergrund uneben ist

glosses: To push or shake abruptly and roughly.

examples.text: The bus jolted its passengers at every turn.

glosses: To knock sharply
To shock (someone) into taking action or being alert

examples.text: I jolted her out of complacency.

glosses: To shock emotionally.

examples.text: Her untimely death jolted us all.

glosses: To shake; to move with a series of jerks.

examples.text: The car jolted along the stony path.

glosses: An act of jolting.

examples.text: Timing your first coffee for mid-morning allows the caffeine to work its magic right as your body’s natural energy starts to wane. Instead of a jolt, you get a smooth, effective lift that carries you through the late morning and into the afternoon.

glosses: A surprise or shock.
A long prison sentence.

examples.text: Just sit down and look around for a while. Notice your cell, John. Take a good look at it, because it is going to be your home for the next ten years. Sure! You have just gotten a ten-year "jolt," John; so settle down and be a good prisoner.

But blow wise to this, buddy, blow wise to this: Never play cards with a man called Doc. Never eat at a place called Mom's. Never sleep with a woman whose troubles are worse than your own. Never let nobody talk you into shaking another man's jolt. And never you cop another man's plea. I've tried 'em all and I know. They don't work.
After three "jolts" in prison, three separate periods of incarceration, Braly decided to try his hand at writing.

"How long did she do after I left the joint" / "About a year or so. They wanted to parole her. […]" Mae wrinkled her forehead. “It's hard to figure out, sometimes.” Again she frowned heavily. “I don't give a damn myself—I'm a thief, and nothing they can ever do will hurt me. But Mrs. Loring, now, she was different. That jolt did hurt her bad. […]"

glosses: A narcotic injection.

translations.source_sense_description: meist über ein Fahrzeug: sich ruckartig, unruhig bewegen, weil der Untergrund uneben ist

glosses: A light blow or jolting collision.

examples.text: His car had a tiny bump with a moving bus.

glosses: The sound of such a collision.

examples.text: He heard a loud bump and saw the front part of his car was broken and the driver of the other car was running to apologise.

glosses: A protuberance on a level surface.
A swelling on the skin caused by illness or injury.

examples.text: It had upon its brow / A bump as big as a young cockerel's stone.

glosses: One of the protuberances on the cranium which, in phrenology, are associated with distinct faculties or affections of the mind. Also (dated, metonymic) the faculty itself

examples.text: Our task is to elevate the character of the people, raising up, in fact, their bump of self-esteem and suppressing the bumps of servility and fury.
the bump of veneration; the bump of acquisitiveness
Another, with the bump of order unnaturally developed, had his folios and quartos all reduced, in binding, to one size, so that they might look even on his bookshelves.

glosses: The point, in a race in which boats are spaced apart at the start, at which a boat begins to overtake the boat ahead.
The swollen abdomen of a pregnant woman.
A post in an Internet forum thread made in order to raise the thread's profile by returning it to the top of the list of active threads.
A temporary increase in a quantity, as shown in a graph.

examples.text: US presidential nominees get a post-convention bump in survey ratings.

glosses: A dose of a drug such as ketamine or cocaine, when snorted recreationally.

examples.text: “They're getting their drugs mixed up,” she said. “If someone did a line of coke, it would be a very different size than if someone did a bump of ketamine, right? So if they're thinking it's cocaine and they do a line, they could go into a k-hole and be completely unable to move for hours. Maybe not hours, but for a while.”

glosses: A disco dance in which partners rhythmically bump each other's hips together.

examples.text: We sing [...] "God Save the Queen" done in mime and finally "Clap Hands, Here Comes Charley" to a Hawaiian rock with Phoebe doing the bump.

glosses: In skipping, a single jump over two consecutive turns of the rope.
A coarse cotton fabric.
A training match for a fighting dog.
The jaw of either of the middle pockets.
Music, especially played over speakers at loud volume with strong bass frequency response.

examples.text: Call me the juice and you know I'm a stunt; ride in the car with some bump in the trunk.

glosses: A short, self-promotional spot on a radio or television station.
A reassignment of jobs within an organization (for example, when an existing employee leaves) on the basis of seniority.

examples.text: For example, chain bumping, in which a bump by one employee initiates a series of consecutive bumps down a progression line before a layoff results, produces the greatest average number of reassignments per redundant employee.

glosses: In the game of khanhoo, the act of claiming a newly discarded card when it is not one's turn, permitted when one can use the card to form a meld other than a sequence.
A minor problem or difficulty.

examples.text: "I'll try my best, but we still have a few bumps to work out," Ryder muttered.

glosses: A sudden movement of underground strata, preceded by a characteristic sound.
To knock against or run into with a jolt.

examples.text: Their car got bumped while they were turning at the junction.

glosses: To move up or down by a step; displace.

examples.text: I bumped the font size up to make my document easier to read.

glosses: To post in an Internet forum thread in order to raise the thread's profile by returning it to the top of the list of active threads.

examples.text: As in [the online forum] carersvoicesnz, certain contributors were more visible, taking the initiative to "bump" the thread to bring it back into view if it went quiet.

glosses: To suddenly boil, causing movement of the vessel and loss of liquid.

examples.text: Heat until the liquid bumps, then reduce the heat and continue the boiling for 1½ hours.

glosses: To move (a booked passenger) to a later flight because of earlier delays or cancellations.

examples.text: Easyjet said the compensation package for passengers bumped off flights was 'probably the most flawed piece of European legislation in recent years' […]

glosses: To move the time of (a scheduled event).

examples.text: A colleague emails with news that her 4:30 meeting got bumped to 3:30.

glosses: To pick (a lock) with a repeated striking motion that dislodges the pins.
To make a loud, heavy, or hollow noise; to boom.

examples.text: as a bittern bumps within a reed

glosses: To spread out material so as to fill any desired number of pages.
To assassinate; to bump off.

examples.text: You know about the night the kid bumped Brody?

glosses: To displace (another employee in an organization) on the basis of seniority.

examples.text: Employees with 2 years or more, and less than 8 years plant seniority, may bump a probationary employee.

glosses: To anger, irritate.

examples.text: After his ancestors had been browbeaten by the Puritans, and his ancestors had been driven out by the early pioneers [...], if he learned that a magnificent bronze statue is to be erected to his ancestors; wouldn't it bump an Indian?

glosses: In the game of khanhoo, to claim a newly discarded card when it is not one's turn, permitted when one can use the card to form a meld other than a sequence.
To play music through a speaker, often loudly and in public.
To encounter and stop, to catch.
To move while bumping up and down, as a cart or car does on rough ground.

examples.text: The car bumped over the dirt road.

glosses: Posted in an Internet forum thread in order to raise the thread's profile by returning it to the top of the list of active threads.
The breeding call made by the bittern; a boom.
Of a bittern, to make its characteristic breeding call.
